records.text: One piece, two jobs. This is a fork: a single piece goes after several targets, and one move may not be enough to save them all.
Simple problem: this lets one of their pieces fork several targets. Before moving, look for the square where that piece could land.
Simple point: a fork was sitting right here, with one piece able to hit several targets, and the move played walks past it.
The main thing is the pin. That piece has its own king right behind it, so it cannot leave the line, and it stays stuck.
Here is the trouble: a pin against the king is now on offer for the other side, and a piece caught in it stays stuck in place.
A pin against the king was the better move, because it would have nailed a piece to its line. Here that piece gets to move freely.
Big idea: a skewer. The front piece is hit, it has to get out of the way, and the piece behind it is left to be taken.
Two pieces are lined up on one line, and now a skewer is on for the other side. Shift the front piece, and the back one is open.
The better move had a skewer in it: hit the front piece, it moves, and the piece behind it is there for the taking. That chance goes by.
The guard goes first. This move hits the defender, and whatever it was holding up is left with no help.
One defender is holding things together, and now the other side gets to knock it out. Look at what that defender holds up before it is gone.
The better move went after the defender. Without it, the piece it guarded would have stood with no help. Here the defender stays.
Simple point: the king is boxed in on its back row by its own pieces, and this move goes straight for that back row. It is a back-rank mate idea.
Simple problem: the king has no air. Its own pieces box it in on the back row, and the other side can aim for mate there.
The king was boxed in on its back row by its own pieces, so a back-rank mate was ready to go. The move played does something else.
The big thing is the pawn. Walk it all the way to the last row so it can be promoted, and follow that walk.
One of their pawns now has a clear walk toward the last row, and if it gets there it is promoted. That pawn needs watching.
The better move cleared a pawn's walk to the last row and a promotion. The move played keeps that pawn where it is.
The front piece steps aside so the piece behind it can join the attack. That is a discovered attack: moving one piece wakes up another.
Their front piece is standing in the way of a piece behind it, and this move lets it step aside so the back one can attack. A discovered attack.
The better move had a discovered attack. Step the front piece aside, and the one behind it joins the attack. Not played here.
A single move, aimed at two things. That is a double attack, and the defense has to deal with both of them.
With this, the other side gets two attacks out of a single move. A double attack like that needs a reply that covers both.
The better move hit two things at once. A double attack was there, and the move played makes no such threat.
A defender has a job. This move drags it off that job so what it was guarding has no cover. That is deflection.
A single defender carries a lot here, and the other side can now drag it away and leave that work undone. That is a deflection for them.
The better move could have dragged a defender off its job. That chance to deflect it is left on the board.
Nothing guarded that piece, so this move takes it. Plain and simple.
The better move takes a piece with no guard on it. The move played leaves it sitting there. Loose pieces come first.
Simple problem: a piece is left with no guard at all, so the other side gets it for nothing.
Simple problem: this moves the only real defender away from a piece. The other side can take that piece now.
The opponent's last move made a threat, and this move leaves it standing; a piece hangs because of it. The other side's move always gets looked at first.
This capture starts a bad trade. The recapture takes back a bigger piece. A trade is only finished when the last capture is counted.
Simple point: a minor piece is out of its starting spot and ready to work.
A different move would have got a minor piece off its home square and working.
Big plus for the rook: the file it stands on has no pawns of either color, so it has a clear road.
A different move would have given a rook a clear road, an open file with no pawns of either color on it.
Half-open file: that is where this rook now stands. Its own pawns are off that file, and an enemy pawn is still sitting there in front of it.
A different move would have set a rook on a half-open file, its own pawns gone and an enemy pawn still there to aim at.
Big thing: a passed pawn. Nothing blocks it with a pawn, not on its file and not on the files beside it.
Another move would have turned a pawn into a passer, its own file and both side files clear of enemy pawns ahead.
The passed pawn walks one step closer to the last row. It was free before. Now it is closer to being a new piece.
A different move would have walked the passed pawn one step closer to the last row.
Simple point: a pawn stands by itself now. With no friendly pawn on the files beside it, no pawn can help guard it.
A different move would have left a pawn standing by itself with no friendly pawn next door on either side.
Simple point: a piece with no guard gets one, so there is one less loose piece to worry about.
A different move would have given a guard to a piece that had none.
Simple point: this piece stands with no guard. That is a weakness, not a loss.
Another move would have taken the last guard away from a piece. A loose piece is a target, not a lost piece.
There is a fresh legal square for the king now. Good to have that room.
With a different move, the king would have had a fresh legal square to step to.
The king castles. It tucks away to the side, and the rook comes over next to it, all in a single move.
Castling was the other option, with king and rook going in the same turn.
This capture takes away the bishop pair. That side is left without one bishop for the light squares and one for the dark.
A different move would have captured a bishop and split up the other side's pair of bishops.
Simple point: doubled pawns. That side has two pawns on a single file now, stacked up, and neither can guard the other.
Doubled pawns would have come from a different move, two pawns of one color stacked up.
This is the big problem: once this move is played, checkmate is forced for the other side. Go back and find where the defense broke.
Simple point: there was a forced checkmate to play, and this move lets it go. When the king is trapped, look at every check first.
Material goes, and the idea holds. Grab the material, and the checked line still works. That is strong.
Simple point: every other checked move lost. This was the one move left standing. Good defense.
Simple point: of every move that was checked, this one alone kept the advantage. The rest let it go and lost.
Simple problem: something is loose, and the reply takes it at once. Look at the reply and find the loose piece.
The best answer gives check. When the king is attacked, that is the first thing to deal with.
The engine likes another move better. Set that move on the board beside this one and compare what the replies do.
This move is weaker than the engine's best. Look at the reply; that is where the cost shows up.
Strong. Of the moves the engine looked at, this one gives away almost nothing.
This is sound. The engine likes another move more, but the value of the position mostly stays.
The human-move model says this is a natural move. It still is not the best one. The engine finds something stronger.
The human-move model does not expect this move. The engine still rates it strong. Unusual can be right.
There was exactly one move that kept the position playable, and it was missed. The human-move model says it was hard to find. Learn it anyway.
Hard to find, by the human-move model, and the other moves that were checked back that up. Keep this one in your memory.
Without this move, the position falls. The human-move model and the other checked moves say it was a hard defense to find. Well held.
The human-move model calls this natural, and it is also the engine's best move. The easy choice and the right choice are the same.
The human-move model calls this natural. The engine calls it strong, though it likes one move a little more.
Almost no time was left on the clock for this move. Little time makes every move harder.
Played fast, while there was still time on the clock.
This move cost a lot of thinking time. That is fine when it finds something.
Simple point: theory knows this move. Knowing the line is one thing. Knowing the position is another.
This is the move where known opening theory runs out. From now on, the players are working it out for themselves.
With this move, the game is playable again after the earlier setback. Good. Keep building from here.
Some of the other side's mistakes helped, and the game is playable again after the earlier setback. Take that, but do not count on it.
The opponent made a slip on the last move, and this move cashes in. Good.
The opponent made a slip on the last move, and this move does not make use of it. When they slip, look for the punishment.
Simple point: this same problem came up earlier in this game. Put the two moments side by side and find what they share.
The piece that was left without a guard earlier is guarded again. Good.
Not one big mistake. A few small slips have added up, and this move is one more of those.
The advantage was kept, move after move, until the game was won. That is how to finish.
Simple point: this same problem shows up in other saved games as well. That makes it worth real study.
Checkmate. The king has no square to go to. Finished.
Checkmate. The king has run out of room. The defense broke earlier, so go back and find that spot.
A draw. The result is settled, but the moves are still worth a look.
Look at the board. Find your move.
Not quite. Look at the board again and try another move.
No result came back for that try. Go back to the move and play it again.
The saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate for the side that played this move.
With this move played, the saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate for the other side.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has more than it had at the start.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has less than it had at the start.
Accepted for this exercise. The moves shown do not give a clear tactical reason, and I won't make one up.
The exercise turns this move down. The moves shown do not give a clear tactical reason for that either.
This move is on the exercise's list of saved answers. In this exercise, that list is the rule.
This move is not on the exercise's list of saved answers. It is not bad chess for that. It is just not what this exercise is after.
Look at this move until it makes sense. Then move on.
Good move. Take the reason with you, not just the move.
This practice is saved, and the review schedule stays the same.
Solved. This recall still stays on the relearning list for now.
Start here, with the position before any of the moves we look at.
Next move. See what changed.
Check. The king is under attack, and that comes before everything.
This move ends the check on the king.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted, and the move gives check.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted. That is checkmate, and the king is trapped.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted, and that same move gets its king out of check.
A capture.
Capture and check together. Both happen in one move.
Something is captured, and it is checkmate. The king cannot get away.
A capture, and the capture is what gets the king out of check.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row, and it is promoted.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row, is promoted, and gives check.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row and is promoted. Checkmate follows, with the king trapped.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row and is promoted. That same move lifts the check on its king.
The king castles and gives check in the same move.
The king castles, and that move is checkmate. The enemy king is caught with no way out.
Watch the fork pay off. One piece goes after several targets, takes one, and this example comes out ahead in material.
Pinned to its king, that piece may not make the capture shown, because stepping off the line would give the king away.
The attacked piece has its king behind it, so it is pinned. Its only moves are ones that still cover the king, so running is hard.
Not one defender may take back, because each of them is pinned to its king. That makes the capture work, and material is won in the line shown.
With its king behind it, the pinned piece is nailed to that line. As these moves go on, it gets taken.
The front piece moves away, and the piece it was covering is taken along the same line.
The check makes the king move aside. The same attacker then takes the piece that stood behind the king.
First the guard goes, and it was the only guard. The piece it was protecting falls later in these moves.
First the defender gets dragged away, then the piece it was protecting gets taken.
The front piece moves, a line opens, and the piece behind makes a capture down that line.
The front piece moves, and the piece behind it is now giving check.
Two checks land on the king in the same move: double check. Nothing but a king move will do against that.
The moved piece makes an attack and opens a line for a second attacker. Here, that second attacker takes what it was aiming at.
The pawn is promoted, and in this example that side ends the line with extra material.
No guard on that piece, so it is taken. In this example, the side that captured ends up ahead in material.
With its last move, the opponent let a relative pin on the attacking piece go. The target did not move, so in the line shown it is taken.
That marked reply is open to the other side as a legal move. Set it up on the board and see what it does to the position.
Before each move, check which of your pieces could be taken with no good way to take back.
Before a quiet move, look for enemy pieces with no guard.
Go through the forcing moves and look for one piece that can hit two valuable targets.
Before a pinned piece moves, find what is behind it: the king, or something worth more.
An attack can go straight through the first piece. Look for a valuable piece lined up behind it.
A defender about to be traded: see what it guards first.
When a blocking piece moves, a line opens behind it. Follow that line.
Two threats from one move: hunt for that. A check counts, and so does a line that opens.
Before a back-row defender moves, make sure the king still has a square to go to.
Count the pawn's moves to promotion, and look at every forcing pawn push.
A defender about to move: first count what it guards. All of that loses its guard when it leaves.
Count the whole trade: what you take, and what they take back.
See whether a forcing trade can pull a defender away from something else it is guarding.
Here, the saved answers are the yardstick. Moves outside that list may still be fine chess.
The replies in these moves are strong ones. A strong reply is not always the only reply.
The material count covers only the line shown, from where it starts. The values used are written in the explanation.
The saved line does not boil down to one simple tactical reason. Run through it move by move and compare how the replies differ. No positional reason is assumed either.
This explanation goes by the exercise's saved answer setting. Which one is set is in the written notes.
The opening line you are studying, one move at a time.
Right. That move is part of what you are studying.
The answer is somewhere in your picked study lines. One of those moves is the answer.
More than one move from your picked opening lines works here. Any of them counts.
There is one move in your study material for this spot. Find it.
Not in the opening lines you picked. Try again.
Your picked opening lines do not have that move. Try again. The study changed, so this saved try leaves its review schedule alone.
Your picked opening lines do not have that move. Try again. Because this position is retired, nothing about its schedule moves.
In mixed Due, any move from this line will do. Dedicated practice wants this one line and no other.
Scheduled recalls ask for the side you picked. One card covers a position that several active studies share.
The saved session needs a reload first. Then the next move.
Now the board plays the checked line.
The solution was revealed, so this try is saved that way. Play it through below.
Second try, and solved. Both go on your record: the miss, then the finish.
Not one wrong move from start to finish. Good.
Not the solution. The right moves before it are still saved.
Right move. The puzzle is not done yet; find the next one.
No rush. Think it through, then move.
The engine has not given me enough here to explain this position.
Review on pause. Start it again below, or push a piece around to look.
Pick a move to review it, or play your own idea on the board.
Simple point: this is a book move.
Opening books carry this move.
Book. Opening theory has this move on record.
Still book.
Book again for this one.
The answer is from the book too.
Still the known line.
More book.
The book again, one more time.
The opening books still cover this.
Book again. Being in the book is not the same as being good.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it walks into a forced mate for the other side. Natural or not, go back and find where the defense broke.
Simple point: there was a forced mate to play. The human-move model calls the move played the natural pick, and the mate slips away. Every check gets looked at first.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, but the reply takes something at once. A natural move still has to survive the reply.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick. The engine still finds something better, and some value goes. Easy-looking moves need checking too.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and now one of their pieces can fork several targets. Look for that square first.
By the human-move model, this is a natural pick. It also lines two pieces up for a skewer. Shift the front piece, and the back one is open.
Simple point: every other checked move lost, and this one held. The human-move model rates it a hard defense, and it was found. That defense held.
Every other checked move lost, and this was the move that kept the game in one piece. By the human-move model and the checked moves, a hard one to find. Strong.
Simple point: this move is the only reason the advantage lasted; every other checked move lost. The human-move model rates it a hard resource to find. Found anyway.
The advantage stayed only because of this move; every other checked move lost. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a hard find. Strong.
Fork. A lone attacker, and a handful of targets. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine marks it strong. Unusual can still be right.
A fork, and the engine's top move. One attacker, more than one target. The human-move model and the checked moves both point to a hard find. Strong.
A pin against the king. The pinned piece cannot leave its line with its king right behind it. The human-move model rates the move unusual; the engine marks it strong.
The engine's top move pins a piece to its king, and that piece stays stuck on its line. By the human-move model, a hard one to find. Strong.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick. It also moves the only real defender off a piece, and the other side can take that piece. Natural, and still a mistake.
This moves the only real defender off a piece, and the other side can take it. One checked move held instead, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Learn that one.

The opponent's last move carried a threat to deal with. By the human-move model this reply is natural, but it leaves the threat standing, and a piece hangs. The other side's move gets looked at first.
The threat from the opponent's last move is still there after this, so a piece hangs. Only one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to find.
The capture looks natural to the human-move model, but the recapture takes back a bigger piece. A trade is only finished when the last capture is counted.
This capture starts a trade where the recapture takes back more. One other checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to find. Count it all the way through.
Fork: a lone attacker against a handful of targets. The human-move model calls it the natural pick, and the engine puts it at the top. Easy and right together.
A fork: one attacker, several things hit. The human-move model calls it natural. The engine marks it strong, with one move above it.
This lets one of their pieces fork several targets. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. That defense is worth learning.
A fork was sitting there, one piece able to hit several targets. The human-move model calls the move played the natural pick, and the fork goes by. Forcing moves first.
The one checked move that held was a fork, with one piece hitting several targets. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Go find that piece.
A pin against the king, and the engine's top move. With its king behind it, the pinned piece cannot get off that line. The human-move model calls it the natural pick. Easy and right together.
A pin against the king, so that piece is chained in place. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine marks it strong, with one move above it.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it gives the other side a pin against the king. A piece pinned like that cannot leave its line.
A pin against the king is now possible for the other side. Only one checked move held up, and by the human-move model it was hard to spot. Learn why it holds.
A pin against the king was the better move, nailing a piece to its line. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the pin goes unused.
A pin against the king was the only checked move that held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Hard defenses are still worth learning.
A skewer, and the engine's top move. Hit the front piece, it moves, and the piece behind it can be taken. Both the human-move model and the checked moves say it was tough to find.
A skewer: the front piece gets hit, and the piece behind it is open once the front one moves. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick. The engine marks it strong.
A skewer: two pieces on a line, and the attack goes through the first to the second. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts it at the top. Right on.
Skewer on a line. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine marks it strong, with one move above it.
Two pieces are lined up, so a skewer is on for the other side. A single checked move held, and the human-move model rates it a tough find. Study that move.
The better move had a skewer: hit the front piece, and the one behind it can be taken. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the skewer stays on the board.
A skewer was in the only checked move that held. It was missed, and by the human-move model it was a hard find. Go back until you can see it.
The guard goes first: this takes the defender, and what it held up is left with no help. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard find.
The target is the guard. Once it is gone, nothing protects what it covered. The human-move model rates the move unusual, and the engine marks it strong.
Take the defender, and what it guarded has no help. Natural to the human-move model, and first on the engine's list. No reason to wait.
The defender is taken, and its protection is gone. By the human-move model, it is natural. The engine calls it strong; one move rates a bit higher.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, but now a defender can be knocked out, and what it guards would have no help.
A defender can now be knocked out by the other side. Just one checked move held, and it was not the one played. The human-move model says it was a hard find.
The better move knocked out a defender and left what it guarded bare. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the defender stays at work.
The one checked move that held took a defender. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to see. Learn that defense.
The king is boxed in on its back row by its own pieces, and this move goes for it. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard find. Strong.
The king's own pieces box it in on the back row, and this move uses that. The human-move model rates it unusual; the engine marks it strong.
The idea is mate on the back row, with the king boxed in by its own pieces. It is the human-move model's natural pick and the engine's first choice.
The king is boxed in on its back row, and this move aims there. The human-move model counts it as a natural pick. Strong, says the engine, though it likes another move a bit more.
The big thing is the pawn and its walk to the last row. This is the engine's top move, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. A pawn like that can decide a game.
The pawn is walking to the last row to be promoted. Not a move the human-move model expects, but the engine marks it strong.
The pawn heads for the last row and promotion. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine likes it best of all. Keep it walking.
The point is the pawn's walk to promotion. The human-move model calls the move natural. By the engine's count it is strong, just not first.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it gives one of their pawns a clear walk toward the last row. That pawn needs stopping early.
Now a pawn of theirs can walk to promotion. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Study that defense.
The better move cleared a pawn's walk to promotion. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the pawn stays put. Count the pawn's steps first.
The one checked move that held would have walked a pawn toward promotion. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find.
The front piece steps aside so the piece behind it can attack: a discovered attack. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard find. Strong.
Shift the front piece, and the piece behind it gets into the fight. A discovered attack. The human-move model rates it unusual, and the engine marks it strong.
A discovered attack: the front piece moves so the back one can attack. The human-move model expects it, and the engine rates nothing above it.
The front piece clears the way for the one behind it. A discovered attack. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine marks it strong, with one move above it.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it lets one of their front pieces step aside for an attack from behind. A discovered attack, right there.
This lets the other side uncover an attack from behind a front piece. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to see.
The better move uncovered an attack: front piece aside, back piece in. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and that attack stays hidden.
The one checked move that held uncovered an attack from behind a front piece. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find.
Two attacks from one move: a double attack, and the engine's top move. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a hard find. Strong.
One move, two attacks. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine marks it strong.
One move makes two attacks, and both need an answer. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts it at the top.
Double attack: a pair of threats out of one move. For the human-move model, this is a natural pick. The engine has it as strong, a step below its top choice.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it hands the other side two attacks from one move. A reply has to cover both.
Now the other side gets two attacks in one move. Just one checked move held, and it was missed. A hard find, by the human-move model.
Two attacks at once was the better move. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the double attack never happens.
A double attack was the only checked move that held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to see.
Deflection: the defender is hauled off, and what it covered is bare. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard find. Strong.
A defender gets dragged off what it protects. The human-move model rates that unusual, and the engine marks it strong.
Haul the defender away, and what it held up is left alone. Natural to the human-move model, and first on the engine's list.
A deflection: a defender is pulled off what it guards. The human-move model calls it natural. Strong by the engine, with one move ranked ahead.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and now the other side can drag a defender off its job. That job would be left undone.
Now the other side can drag a defender off its job. Only one checked move held up, and by the human-move model it was hard to spot.
The better move dragged a defender off its job. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and that defender keeps working.
The one checked move that held was a deflection, dragging a defender away. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find.
Nothing guarded that piece, and this move takes it. The engine's top move, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Seen and taken.
An unguarded piece, collected. Unusual to the human-move model, strong to the engine.
Nothing guarded that piece, and the move takes it. It is the human-move model's natural pick and the engine's first choice. That is all there is to it.
That piece was loose, so the move collects it. By the human-move model, it is natural. The engine marks it strong, with one move above it.
The better move picked up a piece with no guard. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the loose piece stays put. Loose pieces first.
The one checked move that held took a piece with no guard. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to notice. A loose piece should never be missed.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and a piece is left loose for the other side to pick up. Natural, and still a mistake.
A piece is left loose, so the other side may scoop it up. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to see. Learn it.
A minor piece gets out and goes to work. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a hard move to find. Development is not always the obvious move.
A minor piece leaves its starting spot to work. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine marks it strong.
A minor piece comes out and starts working. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine likes it best of all. Plain and right.
A minor piece leaves its starting spot. The human-move model counts it as a natural pick. The engine calls it strong; one move rates a bit higher.
The rook gets a clear road: an open file. The human-move model and the checked moves both point to a hard find. Now use that road.
Open file for the rook, not a pawn on it. The human-move model rates it unusual, and the engine marks it strong.
Rook on the open file, clear road ahead. The human-move model expects it, and the engine rates nothing above it.
An open file, and the rook settles there. For the human-move model, this is a natural pick. Strong, says the engine, though it likes another move a bit more.
The rook's file is half-open: none of its own pawns, an enemy pawn still there. Both the human-move model and the checked moves say it was tough to find.
Half-open file for the rook, with an enemy pawn on it to press. The human-move model would rarely go for it; the engine still marks it strong.
Half-open file: the rook's own pawns are off it, an enemy pawn ahead. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts it at the top.
